claims.claim: By the best cell counts we have, you are about half human.
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, 'Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body', PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text and Table 3 read in the PMC JATS XML (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov OAI record oai:pubmedcentral.nih.gov:4991899); Hatton et al. 2023, 'The human cell count and size distribution', PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text read in the PMC JATS XML (oai:pubmedcentral.nih.gov:10523466).
claims.note: The figure holds for the 70 kg reference man only: 30/(30+38) = 44% (Sender), 36/(36+38) = 49% (Hatton male with Sender's bacteria). 'you' is unqualified, and the hook card does not name the body either. Sender Table 3: 'ref. woman | 63 | | 3.9 | 4.5 | 480 | 0.92 | 21 | 44 | 2.2', i.e. 21/65 = 32% human; young infant 30%, infant 36%, elder 37%, obese 42%. Sender: 'the B/H ratio varies by up to 2-fold across those different population groups from a low of 1.3 to a high of 2.3.' The script's own SOURCES says the reference woman is 'about a third human' and that this is why the screen names the body, but the naming comes only on the next card. For about half the audience, a third is not 'about half'. The authors' one-line summary ('the typical adult human body consists of about 30 trillion human cells and about 38 trillion bacteria') generalises in the same way, but their Table 3 contradicts it for women. 'By the best cell counts' (plural) is fair: Sender and Hatton are the two peer-reviewed censuses, and Hatton's intro says counts are 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells'. Change: either name the body in the hook ('By the best cell counts we have, a typical man is about half human', with 'TYPICAL 70 KG MAN' on the first card from frame one), or use a wording that is true for every Table 3 group and for Hatton: 'By the best cell counts we have, fewer than half your cells are human' (man 44-49%, woman 32-39%, max of any group 44%).

claims.claim: What a viewer who swipes away at second two leaves believing: 'I, whoever I am, carry about as many bacterial cells as human cells' (and possibly 'half of me is bacteria').
claims.source_checked: Sender 2016 Table 3 and Fig 3 legend (PMC JATS XML); Hatton 2023 (PMC JATS XML)
claims.note: The by-mass misreading is headed off: 'by ... cell counts' is spoken and 'by count' / 'BY CELL COUNT' is on screen during the hook. The 'whoever I am' reading fails A4 for women and children (see n=1: reference woman 21 human vs 44 bacteria trillion, B:H 2.2). Change: same fix as n=1. The body qualifier (or the 'fewer than half' wording) has to be in the first sentence or the first card, not only on the second card.

claims.claim: ABOUT HALF HUMAN / best estimates, by count
claims.note: Same issue as n=1 (A4, A6): 'by count' and 'best estimates' are correct framing, but the card carries no body qualifier, and 'typical 70 kg man' appears only on the following card. Change: add 'typical 70 kg man' to this card, or change it to match a reworded hook (e.g. 'LESS THAN HALF HUMAN').

claims.claim: BY CELL COUNT / ABOUT HALF / scrap 'BEST ESTIMATES'
claims.note: Same as n=1 and n=3: the scrap 'TYPICAL 70 KG ADULT MAN' comes later, after the counters. Change: bring the 'TYPICAL 70 KG ADULT MAN' scrap into the hook beat, or match a reworded hook.

claims.claim: Leonardo's Vitruvian Man split at 44%
claims.source_checked: Sender 2016 Table 3 (ref. man total human cells 30, total bacteria 38, x10^12)
claims.note: 30/68 = 44.1%, the reference-man figure. This is accurate for the 70 kg man only, which ties it to the n=1 fix. Hatton's figure would give 49%.

claims.claim: Title: 'By the best cell counts, you are about half human'
claims.note: Same as n=1. The title stands alone (E2/A4) with no body qualifier, and for a reference woman Sender gives 32% human. Change: 'By the best cell counts, a typical man is about half human' or 'By the best cell counts, fewer than half your cells are human'.

claims.claim: About thirty trillion of your cells are yours.
claims.source_checked: Sender 2016 full text; Hatton 2023 full text (PMC JATS XML)
claims.note: Sender: 'This leaves us with 3.0·10^13 human cells in the 70 kg "reference man," with a calculated 2% uncertainty and 14% CV'. Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg, 176 cm, 20 to 50 y), which is within 'about thirty' (20% off, inside A3's limit). The SOURCES block records the disagreement. Confirmed for the 70 kg man, who is named on screen at this beat ('typical 70 kg man (2016 count)'). For a reference woman the counts are 21 (Sender) and 28 (Hatton) trillion.

claims.claim: 30 TRILLION / typical 70 kg man (2016 count)
claims.note: 3.0·10^13 for the reference man ('between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height'). 'Typical' glosses Sender's 'standard reference man', and the authors' own summary says 'the typical adult human body consists of about 30 trillion human cells'. The year label correctly flags it as the 2016 count.

claims.claim: Counter '30 TRILLION', 'YOURS', scrap 'TYPICAL 70 KG ADULT MAN'
claims.note: The figure is Sender's (3.0·10^13), and 'adult' fits the 20-30 y reference man. But Look 2 shows a bare '30 TRILLION' with no '(2016 count)' or 'about', while the newer census gives ≈36 trillion. SOURCES entry 2 justifies the 30 by saying 'on screen the 30 trillion is marked "(2016 count)"', which is true only of Look 1. Change: add a '2016 COUNT' scrap or 'ABOUT' to the Look 2 counter, or correct SOURCES entry 2 to say only Look 1 marks it.

claims.claim: Thirty-eight trillion are bacteria.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 1 '38 TRILLION' / 'bacteria'; Look 2 counter '38 TRILLION', 'BACTERIA'
claims.note: Abstract: 'We estimate the total number of bacteria in the 70 kg "reference man" to be 3.8·10^13.' The paper uses 'bacteria' for all microbial cells: 'Bacteria overwhelmingly outnumber eukaryotes and archaea in the human microbiome by 2–3 orders of magnitude ... We therefore sometimes operationally refer to the microbial cells in the human body as bacteria.' Hatton does not re-count bacteria; it cites Sender (its ref. 17).

claims.claim: False-coloured E. coli SEM shown for 'BACTERIA'
claims.source_checked: label checked against Sender 2016; image content is an illustration, not sourced
claims.note: Confirmed as an illustration only. E. coli is a bacterium and the label says only 'BACTERIA'. Neither paper names species, and E. coli is not a dominant gut species. A pedant could object if the image reads as 'these are your 38 trillion'. Optional: use a generic or mixed gut-flora image.

claims.claim: But put them all on a scale, and those bacteria weigh about two hundred grams.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 1 scale '200 g' / 'in a typical 70 kg man'; Look 2 'ON A SCALE', 'ALL 38 TRILLION', '200 GRAMS', kitchen scale with 200 g ringed, balance scale
claims.source_checked: Sender 2016 full text and Fig 3 legend
claims.note: 'we get a contribution of about 0.2 kg (wet weight) from bacteria ... we conclude that there is about 0.2 kg of bacteria in the body overall.' Abstract: 'their total mass is about 0.2 kg'. Fig 3 legend: 'amounting to only 0.2 kg, which is about 0.3% of the body weight'. This is wet mass, which is what a scale reads. The balance-scale image should not show bacteria outweighing or matching human cells (they are 0.2 kg against ≈46 kg of human cell mass).

claims.claim: 38 TRILLION BACTERIA / far smaller on average
claims.note: 'the average mass of a gut bacterium of about 5 pg (wet weight...)'. Red blood cells are 'among the smallest cell types in the human body with a volume of about 100 μm^3' (~100 pg), and there is '≈46 kg of cell mass' over 3.0·10^13 human cells (~1.5 ng average). So a bacterium is ~20x lighter than a red cell and ~300x lighter than the average human cell (arithmetic on the paper's figures). Sender: 'bacteria have a minor contribution in terms of mass, but a cell count comparable to all human cells combined'.

claims.claim: And your own cells are not what you picture.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 2 'YOUR CELLS', 'YOUR OWN CELLS', 'NOT WHAT YOU PICTURE' over an animal-cell diagram; cheek-cell micrograph
claims.note: Framing line, confirmed as framing. Its factual content is that the typical textbook nucleated cell is not the majority: 'almost 90% of the cells are estimated to be enucleated cells (26·10^12 cells), mostly red blood cells and platelets', and 'The striking dominance of the hematopoietic lineage in the cell count (90% of the total) is counterintuitive'. The paper's own word 'counterintuitive' supports 'not what you picture'.

claims.claim: YOUR 30 TRILLION / counted, not weighed
claims.note: Framing label, confirmed as framing. Sender contrasts count with mass: 'the evident discordance between contributors to total cell mass and to cell number'.

claims.claim: Most of them are red blood cells.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 1 'MOSTLY RED BLOOD CELLS' / '25 of 30 trillion (2016 count)'; Look 2 'MOST', 'RED BLOOD CELLS', SEM of red blood cells
claims.source_checked: Sender 2016 full text; Hatton 2023 full text
claims.note: Sender: 'This led to a total of 2.5·10^13 red blood cells (SEM 2%, CV 12%)' and 'The cell count is dominated by red blood cells (84%)'. Hatton: 'Cell counts are dominated by red blood cells and platelets ... nonnucleated blood cells (≈29 trillion)' of ≈36 trillion. Hatton's main text gives no red-cell-only figure, so 'most' on Hatton is an inference (platelets would have to exceed ~11 trillion to break it). The cited 2016 figure carries the claim.

claims.claim: By count, your cells are mostly blood.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 1 '30 TRILLION' / 'yours, mostly blood'; Look 2 'BY COUNT', 'MOSTLY BLOOD'
claims.note: Sender: 'we identify the dominant role of the hematopoietic lineage to the total count (≈90%)'; 'the body includes only 3·10^12 non-blood human cells, merely 10% of the total'. Hatton: 'Cell counts are completely dominated by red blood cells, platelets, and tissue resident white blood cells, while cell biomass is dominated by muscle and fat'. The line is correctly limited to 'by count'.

claims.claim: And their passengers roughly match them, cell for cell.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen Look 1 '38 TRILLION' / 'passengers'; Look 2 'ROUGHLY EVEN', 'CELL FOR CELL'
claims.note: 'we can give an updated estimate of B/H = 1.3, with an uncertainty of 25% ... This B/H value of about 1:1 (with the associated uncertainty range) should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values'. Confirmed for the 70 kg man, who has been named on screen by this point. For the reference woman (B:H 2.2) 'roughly even' would not hold, so if the hook is reworded to 'fewer than half', keep this line tied to the typical man.

claims.claim: Unit chart of 68 dots: 30 human (25 of them red blood cells), 38 bacteria
claims.note: Ref. man 30 human, 38 bacteria (x10^12); 2.5·10^13 red blood cells. It is a count chart with one dot per trillion, not a mass or size chart, so it does not need a not-to-scale note.

claims.claim: Caption: 'In a typical 70 kg man, about 30 trillion cells are human and about 38 trillion are bacteria. The bacteria weigh about 200 grams.'
claims.note: 3.0·10^13, 3.8·10^13, 'about 0.2 kg', all for the 70 kg reference man. The caption is qualified correctly.

claims.claim: Description: 'For a 70 kg reference man, Sender, Fuchs & Milo (2016) count about 30 trillion human cells and 38 trillion bacteria, about 1 to 1 and not the 10 to 1 once quoted'
claims.note: 'This B/H value of about 1:1 ... should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature'. The 10:1 traces to a 1970s estimate ('only consists of a sentence-long "derivation"'). Outside section A: E4 wants a condensed source list, and the description names Sender but not Hatton ('a 2023 census').

claims.claim: Description: 'a 2023 census puts the human cells nearer 36 trillion. Either way it is about half and half.'
claims.note: Hatton: 'we estimate total body counts of ≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg). That gives 44% (Sender) or 49% (Hatton) human for the 70 kg man named in the previous sentence, so 'about half and half' holds in that context.

claims.claim: Description: 'By count most human cells are red blood cells; by mass, muscle and fat dominate.'
claims.note: Sender: 'The cell count is dominated by red blood cells (84%) ... In contrast, 75% of total cell mass is composed of two cell types, fat cells (adipocytes) and muscle cells (myocytes)'. Hatton: 'cell biomass is dominated by muscle and fat (myocytes and adipocytes)'.

claims.claim: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, 'Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body', PLoS Biology 14(8): e1002533 (2016), doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533; 'reference man' (20-30 years old, 70 kg, 170 cm)
claims.source_checked: PMC JATS XML front matter and text
claims.note: Title, volume 14, issue 8 and e-location e1002533 match. 'Reference Man is defined as being between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height.'

claims.claim: 3.0e13 human cells (2% uncertainty, which the authors say 'might be too optimistically low'), 3.8e13 bacteria, a ratio B/H = 1.3 with 25% uncertainty, which they call 'about 1:1'
claims.note: 'with a calculated 2% uncertainty and 14% CV. We note that the uncertainty and CV estimates might be too optimistically low'; 'B/H = 1.3, with an uncertainty of 25% and a variation of 53%'; 'This B/H value of about 1:1'. The quotations are accurate.

claims.claim: 'The only count that pairs human cells and bacteria for the same reference body'
claims.note: Confirmed within the cited literature, not as a full survey. Hatton names two prior whole-body counts, refs 16 (Bianconi 2013, Ann Hum Biol) and 17 (Sender 2016), 'with an approximately equal number of bacteria cells (17)', so only Sender pairs both. Hatton itself does not count bacteria.

claims.claim: Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120 (2023): '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg, 176 cm, 20-50 y), '≈28 trillion in the female'; earlier studies 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells'; cites Sender for 'an approximately equal number of bacteria cells'
claims.note: Volume 120, issue 39, e2303077120. 'we estimate total body counts of ≈36 trillion cells in the male, ≈28 trillion in the female'; 'Male, (70 kg, 176 cm in height and 20 to 50 y of age)'; 'total counts converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells (16, 17), with an approximately equal number of bacteria cells (17)'. Ref 17 is Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016. The quotes are verbatim.

claims.claim: 30 of 68 trillion is 44% human (Sender), 36 of 74 is 49%; Sender's reference woman is about a third human (21 and 44 trillion)
claims.note: 44.1%, 48.6% and 21/65 = 32.3% are correct. The block correctly says the screen must name the body, but the hook does not (see n=1 to n=4).

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 1: red blood cells counted as cells by both papers; against nucleated cells only, bacteria outnumber them about 10:1 ('a question of definition'); bacteria 'operationally'; archaea and eukaryotes 2-3 orders of magnitude fewer
claims.note: Sender: 'if one chooses to compare the number of bacteria ... to the number of nucleated human cells (≈0.3·10^13), the ratio will be about 10:1'; 'seems to be a question of definition. We view red blood cells as bona fide cells'. Hatton's ≈36 trillion includes the ≈29 trillion nonnucleated blood cells. The 'operationally' quote and '2–3 orders of magnitude' are verbatim.

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 2: 'Hatton's 36 trillion is within "about thirty" at A3's limit, and on screen the 30 trillion is marked "(2016 count)"'
claims.source_checked: on-screen text supplied for Look 1 and Look 2
claims.note: The rounding part is fine. The screen part is true for Look 1 only; the Look 2 counter '30 TRILLION' has no year or 'about'. Change: mark the Look 2 counter (see n=9) or narrow this sentence to Look 1.

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 3: 3.8e13, nearly all in the colon; Sender treats its colon estimate as 'in some respects ... an upper limit'
claims.note: 'the contribution to the total number of bacteria from other organs is at most 10^12'; 'In some respects, the estimate we performed of multiplying observed fecal bacteria density with colon content volume can be considered an upper limit.'

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 4: '~0.2 kg (Sender) ... Sender also revises an earlier figure of 1-3 kg, which came from a 2012 NIH news release.'
claims.note: The 0.2 kg is confirmed. Sender: 'significantly updating previous statements that 1%–3% of the body mass is composed of bacteria or that a normal human hosts 1–3 kg of bacteria [25]', where [25] is 'NIH. NIH Human Microbiome Project defines normal bacterial makeup of the body ... 2012'. Sender cites the release as an example of the statement, not as its origin. Change: 'Sender revises earlier statements of 1-3 kg (1-3% of body mass), citing a 2012 NIH news release.'

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 5: Sender 'The cell count is dominated by red blood cells (84%)', 2.5e13 of 3.0e13; Hatton non-nucleated blood cells (red cells and platelets) ≈29 of ≈36 trillion; 'Most' holds on both
claims.note: The quotes and figures are accurate. For Hatton, 'most' is inferred from the combined red-cell-plus-platelet figure, since its main text gives no red-cell-only count (see n=16).

claims.claim: SOURCES entry 6: '75% of total cell mass is composed of two cell types, fat cells (adipocytes) and muscle cells (myocytes)' (Sender; Hatton agrees); red blood cells 'among the smallest cell types in the human body'
claims.note: Both quotes are verbatim in Sender. Hatton: 'cell biomass is dominated by muscle and fat (myocytes and adipocytes)'.

claims.claim: 'Two peer-reviewed counts, read in full by an independent fact-check (18 Nov 2026)'
claims.note: Both papers were read in full text (PMC JATS XML) in this pass on 2026-11-18. Europe PMC (www.ebi.ac.uk) and journals.plos.org also responded.
